results.title: Out of tune, out of line
results.description: THE world is witnessing calamitous wars, which are recasting the way diplomacy and economic ties have hitherto been conducted. India is caught in the vortex of chaos. One would have tho­u­­ght that in his Independence Day address on Sat­urday, which marked the 79th anniversary of freedom from Britain, Prime Minister Narendra Modi would discuss the fallout of the crisis and prepare the nation for the air pockets ahead. Instead, he was busy supervising a divisive song the Constituent Assembly had warned against in 1950. Russia’s all but declared war with Nato and Iran’s taming of the US and Israeli militaries are indeed tectonic events. In their wake, India’s future as a regional power with global aspirations is at stake. The defence pact Pakistan signed with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye has crucial implications, too, for the security bundobust in and beyond the oil-rich West Asia. Also, Modi has been tasked with hosting a potentially landmark BRICS summit next month, bringing together Russia, China and influential member states that are involved in or watching the Gulf conflict, with key members ranged against each other. Will the BRICS meeting set the tenor for the arriving changes or is India planning to play the spoiler? India’s moral crisis deepened when Amnesty International said New Delhi had sent Israel 2,596 shipments of military ordnance, which could be used in the Gaza genocide. Modi, on his part, has already declared India’s stand by visiting Israel just before the assassination of Iran’s spiritual leader on Feb 28. Like India’s foreign policy, the singing of Vande Mataram was poorly timed. The recent Cockroach protests revealed that Indians are getting weary of Modi’s primeval preference for pitting the people against each other. However, the song evidently failed to shift the focus from the urgent issues of unemployed youths, rampant corruption, including the notorious heist at the Ram temple in Ayodhya, and unintelligent foreign policy choices imposed on harassed citizens. Why does the Congress party get cold feet in challenging deliberately foisted faux religiosity? It was troubling, though, to see the opposition Congress party looking pulverised over the divisive song. Home Minister Amit Shah accused Sonia Gandhi of seeking to stop its singing at a Congress event to mark Independence Day. The Congress made it worse by issuing an embarrassing denial that anyone tried to stop the song. The Gandhi family — Rahul, Priyanka and Sonia Gan­­dhi — have been forceful critics of Modi’s ties with Benjamin Netanyahu and his genocide in Gaza. Rahul Gandhi is widely accepted as an agreeable champion of the hoi polloi. He speaks clearly and forcefully on burning issues like corruption, a stymied education policy, the targeting of the poor, farmers’ distress and alleged rigging of elections. He has notably also asked why, since his gre­at-grandfather Jawaharlal Nehru spent 12 years in British jails before becoming a great world leader, he should not be ready to go to jail for 10 years. Bravado apart, the focus should be on sending the erring opponents to justice. But why does the Congress lose its wits when it comes to frontally challenging Hindutva? The Gandhis routi­nely name the BJP and the RSS as fatal for democracy. Why, then, does the party get cold feet in challenging deliberately foisted faux religiosity? Why is it an ordeal for the Congress to take the stand expected of it, undeterred by any electoral consequences? It’s a Hindutva myth, of course, that Muslims have some special aversion to the controversial lines of Vande Mataram. The discomforting fact for Hindutva, which the Gandhis may wish to share with the party, is that a majority of Indians, including Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, Christians, Parsis, and above all, Arya Samaj Hindus and swathes of tribespeople among others, do not subscribe to the worship of deities mentioned in the uncensored stanzas of Vande Mataram. Its patronage by the Modi government impertinently ignores the separation of religion from the functioning of the secular state that India was conceived to be when it acquired a republican constitution in 1950. That’s how the song was trimmed — to keep the patriotic fervour in the first two stanzas while removing the divisive religious references in the remaining lines. A tuneful Vande Mataram used to be rendered every morning on Akashvani, the state-run radio, without any trouble. It was composed and sung at a Congress function in 1911 in the soothing Raag Desh by Rabindranath Tagore. Vishnupant Pagnis later sang it in Miyan ki Sarang, while Omkarnath Thakur and V.D. Paluskar composed it in other lilting tunes. It was Tagore, author of Indian, Bangladeshi and Ceylonese anthems, who suggested that Vande Mataram be trimmed to accord with the sentiments of India’s multicultural and multireligious patriots. For the record, the 1872 song was part of a Ben­gali novel that described Muslims as the enemies of the motherland and in which the Muslim ruler of Bengal was depicted as the cause of misfortune for the Hindu ascetics, the Santans. Anandmath started a troubling communal canard by airbrushing the militant role of Muslim fakirs who fought shoulder to shoulder with the Hindu sanyasis against the British and their Indian agents. The song’s ongoing misuse by Hindutva practitioners ignores the fact that the ancient Vedic religion, the fountainhead of Hinduism, did not worship Durga or any other goddess in the song. The Arya Samajis emphasised the Vedic origins of Hinduism and banished idol worship from their practice of the religion altogether. Thus, the RSS in recent years has been emphasising its proximity to the Sanatan Dharma. The BJP support for the mostly Sanskrit song would quite likely find most of its supporters struggling to recite or sing it in tune. But Gandhiji, too, was a follower of the Sanatan Dharma, and he was involved in relieving the song of its religious references while keeping the patriotic stanzas intact. It is an unresolved contradiction within the Sanatan fold that Gandhi and his killers shared the same scriptures and drew totally opposite conclusions from their readings. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi. jawednaqvi@gmail.com Published in Dawn, August 18th, 2026

results.title: Transylvania's fortified churches face fragile future
results.description: A view of the fortified church in the village of Cincsor, Romania, on August 8, 2026. Photo by DANIEL MIHAILESCU / AFP Built in the Middle Ages to provide shelter from attacks, Transylvania's fortified churches risk crumbling despite efforts to preserve and breathe new life into them. In a stark reminder, the outer wall of a historic church in the village of Mosna in central Romania -- visited by Britain's King Charles III in 1998 -- collapsed one night in June. Since then, Mariana Rempler, the village's last woman from the German-speaking Saxon minority, lives in fear that the church -- which attracts 4,000 visitors a year -- could also lose one of its towers. "I felt a great pain inside me. It was as if I had collapsed at the same time with that wall," the 74-year-old told AFP, recalling the incident with tears in her eyes inside the church where she herself was baptised and wed. Mosna is one of the over 160 churches fortified with outer walls in Transylvania, built by the German minority so that the population in the then disputed border territory could take refuge from Tatars and Ottomans. As the Saxons left Romania, many to escape the communist dictatorship of Nicolae Ceausescu, several churches deteriorated with no one left to look after them. They are among historic monuments and other buildings in the eastern European country -- one of the continent's poorest -- to fall victim to neglect and decay. New concept for survival Even edifices like Mosna, which underwent renovation after the fall of communism in 1989, remain in danger, with funds for more work difficult to find. Out of the 300,000 Saxons that lived in Transylvania before World War II, only about 10,000 remain today. About half of all fortified churches -- around 80, including Mosna -- have undergone restoration work in the last 35 years or will do over the next five years, Cristian Cismaru, manager at the Fortified Churches Foundation, told AFP. The foundation works with the Evangelical Church in Romania to preserve the historic monuments with grants and donations. Some 85 percent of the money comes from the European Union. "I don't think we'll be able to address the other half of our heritage in our lifetime. That will be left for future generations," Cismaru told AFP at a brunch he organised with the local community for tourists, followed by a tour of the church in the village of Cincsor, 60 kilometres (40 miles) southeast of Mosna. He explained to participants that a third of the 30-euro ($35) entry ticket would be donated to a local development project. "Our role, those of us who live in Transylvania, regardless of nationality, race or religion, is to continue to look after these monuments," he said. "We want to breathe new life into these fortified churches." Cismaru added that many of the churches need "a new concept for their survival", since they can no longer function just as places of worship. One proposal is to turn them into cultural spaces. Earlier this month, fortified churches hosted dozens of events as part of the largest annual festival in Romania, dedicated to promoting the Saxon heritage, which drew a record of almost 10,000 visitors this year, according to organisers. Photos of scattered bricks In Mosna, mayor Dumitru Nutu says that after the wall collapsed even more tourists come to see the church, the village's main attraction. "I keep seeing them from the town hall window. They're all taking photos of the broken wall," Nutu told AFP. Hundreds of scattered bricks, covered by a plastic sheet, are piled at the foot of the endangered tower, which was propped up with wooden beams in 2017. "We reckon repairs will no doubt be carried out," said Francois Regis, a 53-year-old French tourist visiting with his wife, who described the church as beautiful and well preserved except for the northern part. "The blend of Gothic and defensive elements is always interesting. All in all, the concept of a fortified church is quite intriguing." Like the tourists, Rempler also takes almost daily photographs of the tower, aiming to document the visible cracks and to urge speedy action. "I'm afraid that in a month or two, that tower won't still be standing" with the wall no longer there to support it, she said. She hopes that the wall collapse will serve as a wake-up call and a solution will eventually be found. "It would be a shame for us to let it fall into ruin." ©Citizen Digital, Kenya

results.title: 10 million years ago, giant 23-foot crocodilians ruled Miocene South America, hunted massive mammals, dominated the food chain: fossil evidence reveals
results.description: The wetlands of ancient South America were vibrant ecosystems, inhabited by extraordinary species. Dominating this landscape were colossal crocodilians, some measuring 23 feet in length. These formidable hunters preyed on large mammals, playing a crucial role in the food webs of their era. Yet, as geological transformations occurred, the era of these majestic reptiles came to an end.

results.title: Madhya Pradesh August 18, 2026, Weather Update: Heavy Rain Likely In 14 Districts Over Next 3 Days; Showers Expected In Others
results.description: Madhya Pradesh is on alert for heavy rainfall, with 14 districts including Rewa and Balaghat under warning. IMD has forecast heavy rain for the next three days, while nine gates of Bargi Dam may open on Tuesday. Over 20 districts are yet to meet their seasonal rain quota, though 15 districts have recorded above-average rainfall.
